steps.name: Before you begin — set the scope out loud
steps.script: Tell her two things before the first item. First: every word in rungs 1–3 is ordinary Arabic, not Qur'an, and she will not recognise any of it — that is deliberate, because a word she can recite is not a word she has read. Second: no tajweed rule is being tested. Ghunnah, ikhfāʾ, madd counts, qalqalah are all out of scope; she has not been taught them. Marking a Unit 3 rule here is the commonest examiner error at this checkpoint. Conditions for all four rungs: unaided — no prompting, no starting syllable, no "look at the shadda" — and plain text, with no colour muṣḥaf, transliteration or annotation.

steps.name: Rung 1 — twenty unseen words
steps.script: 20 unseen, fully-voweled words of 4–8 letters, non-Qur'ānic. Genuinely unseen: not "not recently practised". Ordinary Arabic vocabulary gives a clean reading score because memory cannot substitute for decoding. Mark each deduction into exactly one cause column (see the mark sheet step), never as a passage total.

steps.name: Rung 2 — ten unseen phrases
steps.script: 10 unseen phrases of 2–5 words, non-Qur'ānic. This is where waṣl-hamzah-when-joining shows up: the hamzah must disappear every time she joins from the previous word.

steps.name: Rung 3 — six unseen sentences, with her own stops
steps.script: 6 unseen complete sentences, non-Qur'ānic, read with stops she chooses. She may plan her stops before reading — planning is a skill this unit taught and it is being assessed, not excluded. Watch the three stop errors specifically: a final ḥarakah kept, a ة read as a t, and a long vowel clipped.

steps.name: Rung 4 — one unseen muṣḥaf page
steps.script: One full page of plain Uthmānī text, Qur'ānic and never read before. Not al-Fātiḥa, not the last page from 2-14, not anything in surahs 105–114 — pick a page from the middle of the muṣḥaf. She will not know the words. Tell her so before she begins; the point is that she is decoding rather than recalling.

steps.name: Mark sheet — one column per cause, not one score per passage
steps.script: A result of "−9 on the muṣḥaf page" is unactionable. Use a row per item and a column per cause: letter/makhraj · tanwīn · sukūn cluster · shadda · madd 2 · madd 6 · līn · waṣl hamzah (join) · waṣl hamzah (start) · stop: ḥarakah · stop: ة · stop: long vowel · stop: placement · pace. Fourteen columns; every deduction gets a tick in exactly one. The column totals are the result that matters — the total across the bottom is only the number. Mark all Jali first, in red; Khafi in yellow. Carry the sheet forward: a cause that cost a deduction at Checkpoint 1, again in weekly sessions, and again here is fossilising, and it goes to the front of the queue whatever the total says.

rubric.criterion: Laḥn Jali — major, clear: wrong letter, wrong makhraj, or a word that is not Arabic
rubric.pass: −2 each. The general test: if a native listener with no tajweed training would notice, it is Jali.

rubric.criterion: Laḥn Khafi — minor, hidden: quality degraded, meaning intact
rubric.pass: −1 each. Detectable by a trained ear only.

rubric.criterion: Self-correction after prompt — she fixes it once alerted
rubric.pass: −1. This is the error that predicts readiness best; see the second pass condition.

rubric.criterion: Examiner has to correct — she cannot fix it even when alerted

rubric.pass: Wrong letter or makhraj · shadda not doubled at all · a madd read short enough to change the word (كَاتِب / كَتَب) · waṣl hamzah pronounced when joining · waṣl hamzah started on the wrong vowel · a final ḥarakah kept at a stop · ة read as a t at a stop · stopping mid-word, which also stops the reading and restarts the item.

Shadda doubled but not held · madd audibly present but short of two counts · līn given a small stretch when joining · long vowel clipped at a stop · uneven, word-by-word pace, counted once per rung and never stacked per word.
Not an error. Out of scope — do not mark it.

(1) Numeric ≥ 70% of the available points across the four rungs, OR (2) no Jali error survives an examiner correction — every major error she made, she could fix when prompted. They are deliberately different tests: the first says her reading is good enough, the second says her internal monitor works, which is the better predictor that Unit 3 will land. A student passing on (2) with a score in the sixties is genuinely ready — she makes errors but she owns them.
